title: Ashtpadi 9, salok: the true names
hook: the salok turns to what the true devotee is like

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi eight: a child in her father's shoes, and a portrait to grow into. Your line was grow into it. Which quality did you try on? Today, ashtpadi nine. Day four hundred seventy.

Every age has its religious job titles. Reverend. Doctor of divinity. Elder. In Guru Arjan's Punjab, around 1600, there were plenty too, and people heard them every day: pandit, the learned one; vaishnav, the devotee of Vishnu; and aparas, the untouched one, a holy man who kept himself ritually apart, never touching anything that might make him impure. Ashtpadi nine takes these honored names one by one. It doesn't mock them. It does something more interesting. It asks what each name would look like if it were true all the way through.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TITLES.` → `PANDIT, VAISHNAV, APARAS.` → `WHAT IF EACH WERE TRUE?`

segments.voice: The salok begins with the last of those names. Whoever keeps the Name enshrined in the heart, and sees God in everyone, and bows to the Master moment by moment: Nanak, that one is the true aparas, and saves all. Notice the swap. The aparas of the day kept apart from other people to stay pure. Guru Arjan's aparas sees God in everyone, which is the opposite of keeping apart. The purity is still there, but it's moved. It's not about what your hands avoid. It's about what your heart holds. The first stanza fills it in: the true aparas is one whose tongue never touches a lie, whose eyes don't look with lust at another's spouse, who loves the company of the holy. The untouched one is untouched by falsehood. That's the pattern of the whole ashtpadi. Each stanza takes a respected title and pours new content into it, a life to match the name. And it says nothing against the people who held those titles sincerely. It just won't let the name do the work by itself. This fits the Sikh path closely. Sikhism has no priestly caste. A granthi who reads in the gurdwara is a respected servant of the community, not a holy class apart, and any Sikh, woman or man, may read the Guru Granth Sahib. So the question ashtpadi nine keeps asking is not what are you called, but what are you like.
screen: `APARAS: THE UNTOUCHED ONE.` · `NOT APART: SEEING GOD IN ALL.` · `UNTOUCHED BY FALSEHOOD.` · `A LIFE TO MATCH THE NAME.` · then, large: `TRUE, NOT TITLED.`

segments.voice: The practice: think what makes a person true. Picture someone with an impressive title, a doctor, a judge, a teacher, a religious leader. Now picture someone with no title at all who is completely trustworthy. Which one would you call at two in the morning? Let that answer settle. Then turn the question round, gently, toward yourself. Not what you're called. What you're like, when no one's watching. Breathe in: the name. Breathe out: the life. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi nine. Its salok names the true aparas: not the one who keeps apart, but the one who sees God in all.
Your line: true, not titled. Today, when someone's title impresses you, ask quietly what their life is like, and then ask it of your own. Day four hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Sikhism has no priestly caste: any Sikh may read the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to live up to a name rather than rest on it.

fork.setup: an aparas of the Guru's day keeps apart to stay pure. what does the salok's true aparas do?
options: holds the Name in the heart and sees God in all.
fork.reveal: the purity moves from what the hands avoid to what the heart holds: Nanak, that one is the true aparas.

original.note: Gurmukhi: aparas, the untouched one; a title of ritual purity the salok gives new content.

trapdoor: what you thought: ashtpadi nine is a list of titles.
what it means: it pours a matching life into each respected name.
what a scholar hears: aparas (a- 'not' + paras 'touch') named ascetics who avoided ritual contact; ashtpadi nine reworks aparas, vaishnav, bhagauti and pandit in turn.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 9, salok and pauri 1 (Ang 274)
sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)

notes: Salok 9 paraphrased: ur dhaarai jo antar naam / sarab mai pekhai bhagvaan / nimakh nimakh thaakur namaskaarai / Nanak oh aparas sagal nistaarai. Confirm.
Pauri 1 details (tongue untouched by falsehood; eyes not looking at another's spouse; love of holy company) paraphrased; confirm.
Aparas described as ascetics who kept ritually apart; framed respectfully toward Hindu practice. Keeper and possibly a Hindu reviewer should check the framing.
Order of titles reworked in ashtpadi 9 (aparas, vaishnav, bhagauti, pandit); confirm.
Audit (2026-10-01): 'sixteenth-century Punjab' changed to 'Guru Arjan's Punjab, around 1600', since Sukhmani is usually dated to about 1602 to 1604.
